#separator:: Web server hacking vs web application hacking?
column2: Module 13 = server/config/patch layer (HTTP daemon, OS, config); Module 14 = app code (XSS, SQLi, auth logic).

#separator:: Directory/path traversal — what does it abuse?
column2: ../../ sequences to escape the document root and read arbitrary OS files (e.g. /etc/passwd).
Traversal escapes the doc root to read outside it; brute forcing guesses existing paths (admin/backup). Different intents.

#separator:: Encoded form of ../ used to evade filters?
column2: %2e%2e%2f (and double/Unicode encodings).

#separator:: XST (Cross-Site Tracing) abuses which HTTP method?
column2: TRACE — echoes the request, reading cookies/headers even if HttpOnly. Mitigation: disable TRACE.

#separator:: Which HTTP methods enable a WebDAV webshell upload?
column2: PUT (write a file) and MOVE (rename to an executable extension) → RCE.

#separator:: Command to list enabled HTTP methods?
column2: curl -s -X OPTIONS -i http://target — read the Allow: header.
Reading Server: / X-Powered-By: response headers (curl -I) to identify software/version.

#separator:: Is banner suppression a real control?
column2: No — it is obscurity. Patching is the control. Suppression only buys time.

#separator:: HTTP response splitting — what is injected and where?
column2: CRLF (%0d%0a) into a response header, forging a second response → cache poisoning / header XSS.
Splitting = CRLF into a response header; smuggling = front-end/back-end desync of request boundaries.
An unkeyed request header reflected into the response and stored by a shared cache.
Server returns raw script text (.bak, .old, .php~, ::$DATA) instead of executing it — often leaks creds.
To hunt backup/source files (config.php.bak) and hidden admin panels for source disclosure.
Scanning a web server for known misconfigurations, dangerous methods, default files, missing headers. Loud, not stealthy.
Fingerprinting the web technology stack (server, framework, CMS).
Content discovery — brute forcing directories/files to find hidden paths.
WordPress-specific enumeration: users, plugins, themes, and versions.
Probe and abuse WebDAV: davtest checks which extensions PUT/exec; cadaver is an interactive DAV client.

#separator:: nmap NSE scripts for HTTP enumeration?
column2: http-headers, http-methods, http-title, http-enum, http-webdav-scan (and http-server-header).
Info gathering → footprinting → mirror site → vulnerability scanning → session hijacking → password cracking.

#separator:: Three common web servers to know?
column2: Apache (Linux, /var/www), Nginx, IIS (Windows, wwwroot, AppPool identity).

#separator:: What runs a webshell after upload — which identity?
column2: The web service account (www-data / IIS AppPool), NOT root/SYSTEM. That boundary is why least privilege matters.

#separator:: Best fix for an unpatched known web-server vuln?
column2: Patch cadence backed by an accurate inventory (not banner suppression or renaming).
Remove samples on deploy and change/vault any default admin credentials.
Disable WebDAV and unused methods (TRACE/PUT); keep doc root read-only; FIM on the web root.
Canonicalize and validate paths; run web root on its own mount; WAF as defense-in-depth.

#separator:: PAM: fix for hardcoded app-pool / service credentials?
column2: Remove the static secret; deliver it at runtime via CyberArk CCP/AAM.

#separator:: PAM: fix for secrets in web.config / config files?
column2: Centralize and rotate them in Conjur; keep no secrets in the web root.

#separator:: PAM: fix for an over-privileged web service account?
column2: Onboard to CPM as a least-privilege service identity and rotate it.

#separator:: Early signal that a webshell was dropped in the doc root?
column2: File-integrity monitoring (FIM) on the document root, plus a read-only doc root and least-privilege account.
T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1505.003 Web Shell.
